comments.name: Rudy Flameng
comments.body: I imagine a major reason for the decline of labor's share of wealth is the shifting nature of labor. What does a worker, say in a factory, actually 'do', and what is that activity's contribution to wealth creation? There was a time when (Western) factories made products. A washing machine company made washing machines by transforming sheets of metal and rolls of copper wire and some other stuff into a functioning domestic apparatus. Today a washing machine is essentially the result of a logistical process in which an array of components coming from elsewhere, usually East Asia, is briefly warehoused and then presented for assembly into a finished product. That is to say, the value added by the assembly process is significantly lower than what the true crafting used to add. To supplement that effect, there is the virtually maximized automation and digitalization that have happened over the past 50 years, and that have moved skills and expertise into machines. What this also means, obviously, is that what is sold as increased worker productivity is nothing of the sort. The output per hour worked has seemingly multiplied, but not because workers have become better at their jobs. In reality a lot of the work is still being done, only off site, where components are made, and the rest of the gain is due to work having been handed off to machines.

I was in 4th grade on 9/11. School started at 9 AM, and every morning before class started the teacher would turn on the local news and let us watch, so that we would become good citizens knowing what was going on the world. That morning the whole class was being super rowdy, and I distinctly remember the teacher yelling “Everybody be quiet, the news is important!” She had no idea what had just happened and turned on the TV. The whole class saw the burning towers and sat there in silence. Then the teacher looked horrified and turned off the TV. 

The principal walked in to our class 10 minutes later and made us swear not to tell anyone else in the school the rest of the day. We had to pretend everything was normal when we all knew something terrible had happened. 

I remember looking up at the sky during recess, processing it all, and seeing how blue it was. To this day, when I see a sky like that I still call it 9/11 blue.

Before and After

Before September 11, 2001, security was largely invisible. 

You could arrive at the airport 30 minutes before departure with family at the gate. No shoes off, no laptops out, no body scanners. A water bottle or pocket knife drew no attention. Office buildings, courthouses, and stadiums required only a ticket or a signature in a logbook. Travel was anonymous.

That ease reflected a quiet belief that we were safe here, insulated by oceans.

I watched the second plane hit live, watched the towers fall, and watched ash-covered people walk uptown for hours. We all knew someone who knew someone. 2,977 people went to work that morning and never came home.

Afterward, the nation changed fundamentally to ensure it never happened again. The Department of Homeland Security was created. Private airport security was replaced by the TSA. Cockpit doors were reinforced. 

What feels routine today felt jarring then, because we remember what it cost to require it.

The “firewall” against the AfD should be understood in the context of German history. The AfD says it has no intention of dismantling the German basic law, the Grundgesetz. But constitutional safeguards cannot depend solely upon political assurances.

Germany experienced two World Wars between 1914 and 1945, followed by extraordinary destruction and human loss. The lesson drawn from that catastrophe was not simply to hope that history would not repeat itself, but to construct institutions capable of resisting the forces that had destroyed Germany’s first democracy.

The Grundgesetz was ratified in May 1949. Its constitutional architecture reflects the principle of “Nie wieder” — Never Again.

From that perspective, a political firewall is not necessarily an assault on democracy. It can instead be understood as one of the mechanisms by which Germany’s post-war democracy protects the constitutional order that was deliberately created after 1945.

The question is therefore not whether the AfD should be silenced. It is whether Germany should ignore the historical reasons why its democratic system contains safeguards against precisely this kind of political danger.

comments.name: Mark Kropf

There is clear evidence of long-term effects after wildfires.   An Indonesian study, the Indonesian Family Life Study of 1997-2007 found that a large wildfire in that Nation created a drop of the mean lung capacity of 20.4 Liters/minute over that 10 year period!
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667278221001073#bib0024
Projections of increased risks of heart attack increases and of cancers also hold for wildfires in studies of Neumann and another study by Grant and Ruckel.    Much of Maui still sees lung problems cropping up from the survivors of the Lahina 3 years ago.

The World Trade Center has ever so many more carcinogens and inhaled particulate matters for lung and circulatory damage as to make projections much the worse to any logically-thinking individual.

I cringed when I heard Christine Todd Whitman declare the area about the WTC safe without respirator masks.   The declaration was totally irresponsible from what I knew as an Internist!

Drywall, electrical insulation and even heavy metals were vaporized and were not magically to be seen as dispersing to no potential toxic effect!

The air may even now register very minute residue of the building collapse, perhaps not toxic, but do we even know the threshold for lung damage all that well?   The current levels may not create much disease, but they likely do see some rare individuals with poor lung response to inflammation at some risk for impaired health from the small residual present.

I felt a little miffed when my midwestern city adopted these, imposing a one-time charge to do so.  

I have changed my mind.  

It is vastly better for sanitation workers and their backs, and for residents who have no business trying to wrestle or carry a traditional trash can to curbside.  It might have kept my father from fracturing his pelvis from
Trying to stand on one leg and stomp the trash down in the trash can.

And while New Yorker’s may be used to tat populations comparable to London during the Plague, it is a bad idea.  

We see rats infrequently in my city.  Raccoons can sometimes get in.

When our Civil War vintage elm was still with us, we did have squirrel(s) who would invest a couple years time to gnaw through the lid so as to have a winter buffet.  

After he managed to get in, a call to city sanitation got us another lid.

But for a year after that, the squirrel would be sit in “V” in the elm, looking through my living room window, glaring at me for negating his hard work.

Adopt these trash bins, and the rats will not be happy.

I am not that empathic.  I worry more about disease than the opinions of ten million rats and their disease-carrying fellow travellers.  I still recommend the bins.

comments.body:
The defining mark of a declining political culture is not fierce disagreement, but the loss of nuance. Contemporary political life has flattened into rigid binaries—left versus right, good versus bad—that replace critical thinking with tribal alignment. When every policy dilemma becomes a zero-sum contest, the intellectual habits required for self-governance vanish. Democratic citizenship depends on a commitment to complexity, shared evidence, and the recognition that public problems rarely yield simplistic solutions. Modern polling and partisan discourse enforce this reductionism, coercing citizens to align rather than deliberate. 

Consider the debate over immigration pit absolute openness against total restriction, ignoring the foundational tension between a nation-state's need for defined borders and its moral duties toward non-citizens. These issues cannot be resolved by partisan slogans; they demand history, law, and reasoned inquiry. 

A healthy republic requires a Socratic disposition: asking "What evidence supports your conclusion?" rather than "Which side are you on?" Without a shared baseline of logic and empirical reality, public conversation devolves into noise and tribal hostility. Sustaining democracy demands resisting instant reactions, refusing false binaries, and choosing instead to ask better questions.

This news, while not surprising, is a devastating blow. Bunch fought the good fight for a long time and, in that time, educated generations of Americans that it was possible to both love our country and question our past. He reminded us that doing so was an important exercise in democracy, not a threat to it. This is a message that needs to be repeated, shouted from the rooftops, in an era where sanitization - the easy way out - is spoken from the highest levels of power.

Honest history should be our right, not our fight. Our nation's students, our citizenry, the world, deserve better.

Thank you for being a champion of truth, Dr. Bunch. You will be missed.

He is truly one of the nation's great museum leaders-- principled, ethical, and dedicated to telling America's story in all its complexities.  He has prioritized the integrity of the Smithsonian and protected his staff as much as he could during these dark times.  This will always be an important part of his legacy.

The news of his resignation is not unexpected, given the intense pressure he has been under.  I was hoping against hope that he could hang on if only to save us from what is likely to happen next-- the appointment of a Trump syncophant.  

Thank you for your strength, integrity and leadership, Secretary Bunch.  May your next chapter be a a happier one.

If our mothers ate too much or too little or drank alcohol or smoked or did drugs we are tagged with hundreds of epigenetic markers that (adversely) modify how our genes function, Even it was our fathers who suffered from stress or smoked or had a bad diet or failed to exercise much we're tagged for life. Studies show behaviours and conditions of life of our grandparents effect our epigenetics. This is not heredity as we understand it, but an imprinting of the life and circumstances of parents, grandparents, and probably beyond, though the signals get too weak to find. Parents have a responsibility to be as fit and healthy and live as healthy a life as possible in order to give the best chances to their offspring.

comments.body: Fantastic article about our attitudes towards living even while being surrounded by the certainty of being mortal. My late father built his dream home on the property that his father-in-law gave him as a wedding gift. He started building on it in 1980 when I was just 14. It was a nice piece of land surrounded by trees but uniquely had a large cemetery right behind our back yard. You could see the tombstones from the windows of the master bedroom and our main bathroom. And to make it really quite interesting many of the German ancestors and relatives on my maternal grandparents were buried there dating back to the mid 19th century. A lot of my teenage experiences were tied up with that place. I first learned how to roll a joint near the Memorial cenotaph and knew a lot of kids who would hang out and even make out after night fell. Interestingly our house was located on the top of a hill just minutes away from the Monroeville Mall where George Romero filmed his 1979 classic Dawn of the Dead; you could see it from the picture windows in our living room in the front of the house. I used to torment my kid brother who was afraid of zombies by first saying that they didn't exist at all, but if they actually do remember that we're well situated on ground zero with our late relatives just minutes away. Needless to say that didn't help.

When I read about the valuations of untested, pre-revenue tech startups, I’m reminded of the fiat currency system, which is often criticized for creating money out of thin air at the whim and discretion of a few institutions.

My guess is that hedge funds, venture capitalists, and bankers probably use their own proprietary formulas and valuation models to derive these figures. Nevertheless, should these private financial institutions be allowed to assign arbitrary monetary values to their own investments and then cash them out through the IPO process in the current manner - especially if this practice instantly creates billionaires and a bunch of brand new upper-middle-class millionaires overnight, causing localized inflation and affordability issues for the general public, even before considering the growing public concern of a potential bubble?

In my opinion, given its potential impact on society, perhaps there should be more public awareness through greater transparency and oversight into the entire process of transforming value on paper into actual monetization in a timely, step-by-step manner.

And as always, there should be no taxpayer-funded socialization of private losses.

As a Tibetan, I found reading this article extremely sad. Although the report is ostensibly about the destruction, loss, and suffering experienced by people on the Tibetan side of the border as a result of the recent disaster, it never cites, quotes, or even mentions a single Tibetan—a native of the land. There is only Tibet, the land, but no Tibetans. Instead, the people quoted and mentioned are exclusively those with Chinese names.
How did it come to this?
One cannot understand the situation without acknowledging the historical and political context: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) entered Tibet in 1950, and Tibet has been under Chinese control ever since. The Chinese presence in Tibet is not simply that of ordinary residents; it is the result of a contested political and military occupation. Yet this article presents that presence as entirely normal, without mentioning the fundamental historical context.
Whether intentionally or unintentionally, this risks normalizing the presence of Chinese authorities and settlers in Tibet while erasing Tibetans from the narrative. In doing so, the article contributes to a rewriting of Tibet’s history that closely mirrors Beijing’s official narrative.

Kuang’s writings remind me of HG Wells’ depiction of future society in The Time Machine. When written in first person, their POV is naive and egocentric; when written in third person, they’re fantasies. In both instances, hapless protagonists make their way through strange, precarious settings, subject to the whims of powerful others. 

Just as Wells’ 1895 work highlighted widespread social and economic displacement in the wake of the industrial revolution, Kuang’s writings reflect the Eloi-like consciousness of many of her leading characters trying to make sense of today’s globalization, artificial intelligence and other disruptive forces. 

The difference between Wells and Kuang is that of analyst (the former) and observer (the latter).

Separately, we have a crisis in quality at true “entry level” pricing for wine in California that is most pronounced red wine.  The cost of good Cabernet land, barrels, labor and overheads across a 2-3 harvest-to-release cycle, now means that the predominant opening price for Cabernet Sauvignon with any character is $40+.  Much like Chardonnay has stared to be interpreted different in places like the Willamette Valley and the West Sonoma Coast, I hope to see greater style diversity in Cabernet emerge. comments.name: Chuck
comments.body: If Ms. Kung were to revisit Taipei next week, I'd recommend she walk into some of the local traditional markets there. One particular market stands out, the Di What Street market. It's the most popular market for local residents to do their shopping for the lunar New Year holiday. It's got a puppet museum and a temple along side with numerous teahouses and restaurants stretching over a street that's 500 meters long at least, not to mention all the winding and narrow alleys running through it. Best of all, visitors can find all kinds of fabrics in the main public building of the market. You can spend an afternoon there going up and down the three-story building hunting for the fabrics that delights you and have it made into the final handkerchief or whatever shape you want to take it back home as a souvenir. You can also have it embroiled with your name on it while you have your oolong or latte inside the same building.
